'''Michael (Mickey<ref name="encyclopedia">{{cite book |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/book/9780081003794/the-encyclopedia-of-mass-spectrometry |title=The Encyclopedia of Mass Spectrometry |isbn=9780081003794 |format= |accessdate= |last1=Nier |first1=Keith A. |last2=Yergey |first2=Alfred L. |last3=Jane Gale |first3=P. |date=6 May 2015 |publisher=Elsevier Science }}</ref>) Barber''', [[Fellow of the Royal Society|<small>FRS</small>]] (3 November 1934 – 8 May 1991) was a British [[chemist]] and [[mass spectrometry|mass spectrometrist]], best known for his invention of [[fast atom bombardment]] ionisation.<ref name="Reid1999">{{cite book|author=Ronald Reid|title=Peptide and Protein Drug Analysis|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=C-LnQHG2ztYC&pg=PA529|date=12 November 1999|publisher=CRC Press|isbn=978-1-4200-0133-4|pages=529–}}</ref><ref name="Green1992">{{cite journal|last1=Green|first1=Brian N.|title=In Memory: Professor Michael Barber FRS|journal=Organic Mass Spectrometry|volume=27|issue=1|year=1992|pages=67|issn=0030-493X|doi=10.1002/oms.1210270119}}</ref>

== Biography ==
[[File:Front Quad, The Queen's College.jpg|thumb|Front Quad, Queen's College, Oxford]]
On 3 November 1934, Barber was born at his family's home in [[Manchester]] at 166 Lodge Lane in [[Newton, Greater Manchester|Newton]]. His family were [[Working class|working-class]] and underprivileged. Barber was one of two boys; his brother Peter was born in 1927. His father, Joseph Barber, was a [[Carpentry|carpenter]].<ref name="Beynon 1996">{{cite journal |last1=Beynon |first1=John Herbert |title=Michael Barber, 3 November 1934 - 8 May 1991 |journal=Biographical Memoirs of Fellows of the Royal Society |date=1 November 1996 |volume=42 |pages=2–9 |doi=10.1098/rsbm.1996.0001 |doi-access=free|s2cid=71325506 |url=https://royalsocietypublishing.org/doi/10.1098/rsbm.1996.0001 |accessdate=17 August 2020|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

He went to [[Manchester Grammar School]]<ref name="encyclopedia"/> and was then educated at [[the Queen's College, Oxford]], obtaining his [[Bachelor of Arts|B.A.]] in 1958 and his [[Bachelor of Science|B.Sc.]] in 1959. There he worked with [[Jack Linnett]] and they designed and built a [[mass spectrometer]] for
the analysis of flames. He married Joan Gaskell in 1958, the couple had three children.<ref name="Beynon 1996"/>

In 1961 he returned to Manchester to work at the Scientific Instruments division of [[Associated Electrical Industries]]. There, he and [[Martin Elliott (scientist)|Martin Elliott]] developed a method to study the fragmentation of ions with a mass spectrometer and started to work on [[X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy]]. In 1973 he took up a lectureship position at [[UMIST]] and was promoted to Professor in 1985. In the same year, 1985, he was also elected a [[Fellow of the Royal Society]]. He remained at Manchester until his death.<ref>{{cite journal|title=Professor Michael Barber FRS. Born 3 November 1934; died 8 May 1991|journal=Rapid Communications in Mass Spectrometry|volume=5|issue=7|year=1991|pages=340–342|issn=0951-4198|doi=10.1002/rcm.1290050709|pmid=1841652|bibcode=1991RCMS....5..340.}}</ref>

==Fast atom bombardment==
[[File:FAB_Schematic.jpg|thumb|right|upright=1.5|Schematic of a fast atom bombardment ion source for a mass spectrometer.]]
[[Fast atom bombardment]] (FAB) is a method of [[ionization]] used in [[mass spectrometry]] that uses a beam of high energy atoms strikes a surface to create [[ion]]s.<ref name="pmid7306100">{{cite journal |vauthors=Morris HR, Panico M, Barber M, Bordoli RS, Sedgwick RD, Tyler A | title = Fast atom bombardment: a new mass spectrometric method for peptide sequence analysis | journal = Biochem. Biophys. Res. Commun. | volume = 101 | issue = 2 | pages = 623–31 | year = 1981 | pmid = 7306100 | doi =10.1016/0006-291X(81)91304-8 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|last1=Barber|first1=Michael|last2=Bordoli|first2=Robert S.|last3=Elliott|first3=Gerard J.|last4=Sedgwick|first4=R. Donald|last5=Tyler|first5=Andrew N.|title=Fast Atom Bombardment Mass Spectrometry|journal=Analytical Chemistry|volume=54|issue=4|year=1982|pages=645A–657A|issn=0003-2700|doi=10.1021/ac00241a817}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Barber M, Bordoli RS, Sedgewick RD, Tyler AN | title=Fast atom bombardment of solids (F.A.B.): a new ion source for mass spectrometry| journal=Journal of the Chemical Society, Chemical Communications | pages=325–7 | doi=10.1039/C39810000325 | year=1981 | issue=7 }}</ref> An energetic beam of atoms or ions will destroy an [[organic molecule]] under conditions typically used to create [[secondary ion]]s. Barber realised that mixing the compound of interest with a vacuum compatible [[Volatility (chemistry)|low-volatility]] liquid such as [[glycerol]] effectively protected the organic molecule and allowed it to be ionized and detected.<ref name="Green1992" /><ref>{{cite book|last1=Gaskel|first1=Simon J.|last2=Gale|first2=P. Jane|editor=Richard M. Caprioli|others=Michael L. Gross|title=The Encyclopedia of Mass Spectrometry: Volume 9: Historical Perspectives, Part A: The Development of Mass Spectrometry|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=aQjtAQAAQBAJ&pg=PA19|date=4 December 2015|publisher=Elsevier|isbn=978-0-08-091325-4|pages=11–12}}</ref> The protecting liquid "matrix" allowed compounds as large as 10,000 Da [[molecular mass]] to be detected. The concept of a protecting matrix was later used in [[matrix-assisted laser desorption ionization]].<ref name="HillenkampKaras1991">{{cite journal|last1=Hillenkamp|first1=Franz|last2=Karas|first2=Michael|last3=Beavis|first3=Ronald C.|last4=Chait|first4=Brian T.|title=Matrix-assisted laser desorption/ionization mass spectrometry of biopolymers|journal=Analytical Chemistry|volume=63|issue=24|year=1991|pages=1193A–1203A|issn=0003-2700|doi=10.1021/ac00024a716|pmid=1789447}}</ref> The FAB technique was employed by Barber, [[Howard Morris (biochemist)]] and co-workers for early peptide sequencing experiments.<ref name="pmid7306100"/>

== Honours and distinctions ==
* Royal Society of Chemistry Award for analytical chemistry and instrumentation (1979)<ref name="Beynon 1996"/> 
* [[List of Fellows of the Royal Society elected in 1985|Fellow of the Royal Society]] (1985)<ref name="Beynon 1996"/> 
* [[American Society for Mass Spectrometry]] – The Distinguished Contribution in Mass Spectrometry Award (1991)<ref name="Beynon 1996"/>

The Michael Barber Centre for Collaborative Mass Spectrometry based at the [[University of Manchester]], is named in honour of him.
